To make the **New Tab button** look like a pill as well, we have to use a little trick. Since WezTerm doesn't allow direct formatting of the built-in "plus" button, we will:
1.  **Hide the built-in button.**
2.  **Append a "fake" pill** to the end of the last tab during the formatting process.

The only limitation is that clicking the "plus" part of the pill will act like clicking the tab itself (selecting it). However, it will create a perfect visual row of centered pills!

```lua
local wezterm = require 'wezterm'
local config = wezterm.config_builder()

-- Color palette
local bg = '#1d2021'
local active_bg = '#d79921'
local active_fg = '#1d2021'
local inactive_bg = '#3c3836'
local inactive_fg = '#ebdbb2'
local hover_bg = '#504945'

config.color_scheme = 'Gruvbox Dark (Gogh)'

-- Font
config.font = wezterm.font('MonaspiceKr Nerd Font')
config.font_size = 12.0
config.line_height = 1.4

-- UI
config.window_decorations = "RESIZE"
config.window_background_opacity = 0.90
config.window_frame = {
  active_titlebar_bg = bg,
  inactive_titlebar_bg = bg,
}

-- Tab Bar Configuration
config.use_fancy_tab_bar = false
config.tab_bar_at_bottom = false
config.hide_tab_bar_if_only_one_tab = false
config.tab_max_width = 50
config.show_new_tab_button_in_tab_bar = false -- Hide the old ugly button

config.colors = {
  tab_bar = {
    background = 'rgba(0,0,0,0)',
  }
}

-- The Powerline Symbols
local LEFT_CAP = wezterm.nerdfonts.ple_left_half_circle_thick
local RIGHT_CAP = wezterm.nerdfonts.ple_right_half_circle_thick

function tab_title(tab_info)
  local title = tab_info.tab_title
  if title and #title > 0 then return title end
  return tab_info.active_pane.title
end

-- Centering and Padding Logic
wezterm.on("update-status", function(gui_window, pane)
    gui_window:set_left_status(string.rep(' ', 4))
    gui_window:set_right_status('')
end)

wezterm.on('format-tab-title', function(tab, tabs, panes, config, hover, max_width)
  local background = inactive_bg
  local foreground = inactive_fg

  if tab.is_active then
    background = active_bg
    foreground = active_fg
  elseif hover then
    background = hover_bg
  end

  local title = " " .. tab_title(tab) .. " "

  local tab_pill = {
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Foreground = { Color = background } },
    { Text = LEFT_CAP },
    { Background = { Color = background } },
    { Foreground = { Color = foreground } },
    { Text = title },
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Foreground = { Color = background } },
    { Text = RIGHT_CAP },
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Text = ' ' },
  }

  -- If this is the LAST tab, append the "New Tab" pill after it
  if tab.tab_index == #tabs - 1 then
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Foreground = { Color = inactive_bg } })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Text = LEFT_CAP })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Background = { Color = inactive_bg } })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Foreground = { Color = inactive_fg } })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Text = ' + ' })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Background = { Color = 'none' } })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Foreground = { Color = inactive_bg } })
    table.insert(tab_pill, { Text = RIGHT_CAP })
  end

  return tab_pill
end)

-- Keybindings
config.keys = {
  { key = 'q', mods = 'CTRL', action = wezterm.action.CloseCurrentPane { confirm = false } },
  { key = 't', mods = 'CTRL|SHIFT', action = wezterm.action.SpawnTab 'CurrentPaneDomain' },
}

return config
```

content.text:
Asked claude how to make the drawing characters thicker because I want: Yes! There are a few ways to make line-drawing (box-drawing) characters thicker in WezTerm, depending on what exactly you're after:

---

### 1. `underline_thickness` (primary option)

The `underline_thickness` setting overrides the base thickness of underlines, and it's also used for rendering split pane dividers and a number of other lines in custom glyphs. So bumping it up will make box-drawing lines thicker too.

```lua
config.underline_thickness = "200%"  -- doubles the default thickness
-- or use pixel values:
config.underline_thickness = 2
```

The caveat, as noted in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/wezterm/wezterm/issues/4610), is that changing `underline_thickness` also modifies how box-drawing characters and other custom glyphs are drawn, so there's currently no way to make underlines thicker without also making those glyphs thicker — they're coupled together.

---

### 2. `custom_block_glyphs` + `anti_alias_custom_block_glyphs`

WezTerm renders many box/block characters itself rather than from the font. You can tweak this behavior:

```lua
config.custom_block_glyphs = true          -- WezTerm draws the glyphs (default)
config.anti_alias_custom_block_glyphs = true
```

Setting `custom_block_glyphs = false` causes border symbols to be rendered as bold (matching how other terminals like Alacritty render them), but it can break some other symbols. Worth trying if you want bolder-looking lines.

---

### 3. `freetype_render_target` for overall stroke weight

Switching to `freetype_render_target = "HorizontalLcd"` gives thicker-looking strokes overall.

```lua
config.freetype_render_target = "HorizontalLcd"
```

---

### Putting it together

A reasonable starting config to experiment with:

```lua
config.underline_thickness = "200%"
config.custom_block_glyphs = true
config.anti_alias_custom_block_glyphs = true
config.freetype_render_target = "HorizontalLcd"
```

The `underline_thickness` option is the most direct lever for line-drawing character weight, but do be aware it also affects underlines everywhere.

Web search results for "wezterm make powerline symbols thicker  ":

I will search the codebase for "powerline" and these specific symbols to understand how they are currently rendered in your WezTerm configuration.
To make the Powerline symbols **** and **** thicker in WezTerm, you can use the `wezterm.font_with_fallback` function to apply a manual **scale** factor specifically to the font that provides these symbols (usually the built-in Nerd Font Symbols).[1]

By default, WezTerm renders these symbols using its internal fallback.[1][2][3] To "thicken" them, you can explicitly define the fallback and increase its scale.[1]

Add or modify your `wezterm.lua` with the following pattern:

```lua
local wezterm = require 'wezterm'
local config = wezterm.config_builder()[1]

config.font = wezterm.font_with_fallback({
  -- Your primary font first
  { family = 'JetBrains Mono', weight = 'Regular' },[1]

  -- Explicitly scale the symbols font to make them appear "thicker" or larger
  { 
    family = 'Symbols Nerd Font Mono', 
    scale = 1.2, -- Increase this (e.g., 1.3, 1.4) to make them thicker/larger
  },
})[1]

return config
```

### Key Adjustments:
1.  **`scale`**: Increasing this value (e.g., from `1.0` to `1.2` or `1.3`) will make the glyphs larger, which effectively makes the lines and curves of the Powerline "bubbles" look thicker and fill more of the cell.[1]
2.  **`custom_block_glyphs`**: WezTerm has a built-in feature that tries to draw pixel-perfect versions of some Powerline symbols.[4][1][2] If the scaling above doesn't give you the look you want, you can try disabling this to force WezTerm to use the font's version:
    ```lua
    config.custom_block_glyphs = false
    ```[1]
3.  **`line_height`**: If the symbols look thick but are getting cut off at the top or bottom, you may need to slightly increase your line height:
    ```lua
    config.line_height = 1.1
    ```[1]

**Note:** The symbols `` (U+E0B6) and `` (U+E0B4) are often part of the "Nerd Font" range.[1] If you find that scaling `Symbols Nerd Font Mono` affects too many other icons, you can use `font_rules` to target specific styles, though scaling the fallback font is the most direct way to adjust their weight.[1]

I've applied a different approach to make those pill caps look thicker! 

Instead of just relying on rendering settings, I've:
1.  **Scaled the Symbols:** Used `font_with_fallback` to explicitly scale the `Symbols Nerd Font Mono` (which provides the caps) to **1.2**. This makes the glyphs larger and fill more of their space, which makes the lines appear thicker.
2.  **Disabled `custom_block_glyphs`:** By setting this to `false`, WezTerm will use the actual glyphs from your font rather than its internal drawing logic. Fonts often have thicker, more hand-tuned versions of these Powerline symbols.
3.  **Retained Rendering Tweaks:** Kept the `HorizontalLcd` target and `underline_thickness` for a heavier overall look.

How do the pill shapes look now? Are they noticeably bolder?

I've noted your manual changes (Wayland enabled and custom block glyphs back on) and will keep them intact.

For your next Nerd Font, here are my top recommendations that are known for excellent rendering and very reliable Powerline symbol support on Linux:

1.  **JetBrains Mono Nerd Font:** The "safe bet." It's incredibly legible, has great ligatures, and its Powerline symbols are perfectly proportioned.
2.  **CaskaydiaCove Nerd Font (Cascadia Code):** Microsoft's modern terminal font. It has a very sleek, high-tech feel and renders exceptionally crisp lines on Linux.
3.  **FiraCode Nerd Font:** Famous for its extensive programming ligatures. It has a slightly more "condensed" look that works well for multi-pane layouts.
4.  **UbuntuMono Nerd Font:** Since you're on Pop!_OS, this font fits the system aesthetic perfectly. It has a very unique character and handles symbols very reliably without alignment issues.
5.  **Iosevka Nerd Font:** If you like a slimmer, taller font. It allows you to fit more code on the screen without feeling cramped.

**My top recommendation:** If you want those pill shapes to look their best, **JetBrains Mono** or **CaskaydiaCove** usually provide the most consistent results across different font sizes.

Would you like me to help you install one of these via `mise` or another method?

This tool executes a given shell command as `bash -c <command>`. To run a command in the background, set the `is_background` parameter to true. Do NOT use `&` to background commands. Command is executed as a subprocess that leads its own process group. Command process group can be terminated as `kill -- -PGID` or signaled as `kill -s SIGNAL -- -PGID`.

      Efficiency Guidelines:
      - Quiet Flags: Always prefer silent or quiet flags (e.g., `npm install --silent`, `git --no-pager`) to reduce output volume while still capturing necessary information.
      - Pagination: Always disable terminal pagination to ensure commands terminate (e.g., use `git --no-pager`, `systemctl --no-pager`, or set `PAGER=cat`).

      The following information is returned:

      Output: Combined stdout/stderr. Can be `(empty)` or partial on error and for any unwaited background processes.
      Exit Code: Only included if non-zero (command failed).
      Error: Only included if a process-level error occurred (e.g., spawn failure).
      Signal: Only included if process was terminated by a signal.
      Background PIDs: Only included if background processes were started.
      Process Group PGID: Only included if available.

local wezterm = require 'wezterm'
local config = wezterm.config_builder()

-- Color palette (Gruvbox Hard)
local bg = '#1d2021'
local active_bg = '#d79921'
local active_fg = '#1d2021'
local inactive_bg = '#3c3836'
local inactive_fg = '#ebdbb2'
local hover_bg = '#504945'

config.color_scheme = 'Gruvbox Dark (Gogh)'

-- Font Configuration
config.font = wezterm.font_with_fallback({
  { family = 'MonaspiceKr Nerd Font', weight = 'Regular' },
  -- Scale symbols to make them appear thicker/larger
  { family = 'Symbols Nerd Font Mono', scale = 1.2 },
})
config.font_size = 10.0
config.line_height = 1.4

-- Rendering Tweaks
config.underline_thickness = "200%"
-- Disable custom_block_glyphs to let the font's own (often thicker) symbols show
config.custom_block_glyphs = true
config.anti_alias_custom_block_glyphs = true
config.freetype_render_target = "HorizontalLcd"
config.enable_wayland = true

-- UI
config.window_decorations = "RESIZE"
config.window_background_opacity = 0.90
config.window_frame = {
  active_titlebar_bg = bg,
  inactive_titlebar_bg = bg,
}

-- Tab Bar Configuration
config.use_fancy_tab_bar = false
config.tab_bar_at_bottom = true
config.hide_tab_bar_if_only_one_tab = true
config.tab_max_width = 50
config.show_new_tab_button_in_tab_bar = true

config.colors = {
  tab_bar = {
    background = 'rgba(0,0,0,0)',
    new_tab = { bg_color = inactive_bg, fg_color = inactive_fg },
    new_tab_hover = { bg_color = hover_bg, fg_color = inactive_fg },
  }
}

-- The Powerline Symbols
local LEFT_CAP = wezterm.nerdfonts.ple_left_half_circle_thick
local RIGHT_CAP = wezterm.nerdfonts.ple_right_half_circle_thick

function tab_title(tab_info)
  local title = tab_info.tab_title
  if title and #title > 0 then return title end
  return tab_info.active_pane.title
end

-- Left padding
wezterm.on("update-status", function(gui_window, pane)
    gui_window:set_left_status(string.rep(' ', 4))
    gui_window:set_right_status('')
end)

-- Tab formatting (Pills)
wezterm.on('format-tab-title', function(tab, tabs, panes, config, hover, max_width)
  local background = inactive_bg
  local foreground = inactive_fg

  if tab.is_active then
    background = active_bg
    foreground = active_fg
  elseif hover then
    background = hover_bg
  end

  local title = " " .. tab_title(tab) .. " "

  return {
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Foreground = { Color = background } },
    { Text = LEFT_CAP },
    { Background = { Color = background } },
    { Foreground = { Color = foreground } },
    { Text = title },
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Foreground = { Color = background } },
    { Text = RIGHT_CAP },
    { Background = { Color = 'none' } },
    { Text = ' ' },
  }
end)

-- Keybindings
config.keys = {
  { key = 'q', mods = 'CTRL', action = wezterm.action.CloseCurrentPane { confirm = false } },
  { key = 't', mods = 'CTRL|SHIFT', action = wezterm.action.SpawnTab 'CurrentPaneDomain' },
}

return config

toolCalls.description:
Replaces text within a file. By default, the tool expects to find and replace exactly ONE occurrence of `old_string`. If you want to replace multiple occurrences of the exact same string, set `allow_multiple` to true. This tool requires providing significant context around the change to ensure precise targeting. Always use the read_file tool to examine the file's current content before attempting a text replacement.
      
      The user has the ability to modify the `new_string` content. If modified, this will be stated in the response.
      
      Expectation for required parameters:
      1. `old_string` MUST be the exact literal text to replace (including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc.).
      2. `new_string` MUST be the exact literal text to replace `old_string` with (also including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc.). Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic and that `old_string` and `new_string` are different.
      3. `instruction` is the detailed instruction of what needs to be changed. It is important to Make it specific and detailed so developers or large language models can understand what needs to be changed and perform the changes on their own if necessary. 
      4. NEVER escape `old_string` or `new_string`, that would break the exact literal text requirement.
      **Important:** If ANY of the above are not satisfied, the tool will fail. CRITICAL for `old_string`: Must uniquely identify the instance(s) to change. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string matches multiple locations and `allow_multiple` is not true, the tool will fail.
      5. Prefer to break down complex and long changes into multiple smaller atomic calls to this tool. Always check the content of the file after changes or not finding a string to match.
      **Multiple replacements:** Set `allow_multiple` to true if you want to replace ALL occurrences that match `old_string` exactly.
